drainage.local_h: Why a sandy Gilmer yard still floods
local: Sand drains fast, so you would expect a Gilmer yard to stay dry. When it does not, there is usually a reason. Sand on top often sits on a clay layer, and rain soaks through the sand, hits the clay and stops. The low spots then stay wet for days after a long rain. A downspout dumping into a flat bed or runoff from a driveway can do the same thing, so we look at the whole lot before choosing a fix.

Rolling ground creates the opposite problem. On a slope of bare sand, fast runoff cuts gullies and carries soil off the lot. For those, we use erosion control, regrading, swales and dry creek beds that slow the water down and move it somewhere it can leave. The rolling terrain around Gilmer often gives water a natural place to go, which is the first thing we look for, because a drain without an outlet is useless.

We walk the property during or right after a rain when we can, and trace where the water comes from and where it sits. Then we pick the right fix: a downspout extension or solid-pipe reroute, regrading and re-sloping away from the foundation, a catch basin, channel drain or pop-up emitter, or a French drain. A standard single run costs $1,900 to $3,000, and full systems run $3,000 to $4,500.

A French drain here is built with sock-wrapped pipe and #57 stone, laid with a steady fall to a real outlet. Cheap corrugated pipe in a rock bag silts up with clay fines in a season or two, then has to be dug up and redone. We fix drainage year-round, though digging goes faster in a dry stretch. Getting it done before spring means one less season with a pond in the back corner.

faq.q: My Gilmer yard is sandy. Why does it still hold water?
faq.a: Sand on top often sits on clay underneath. Water soaks through the sand fast, hits the clay and stops, so low spots stay wet. We look at the grade and where the water collects, then fix it with regrading, a French drain or a swale that moves it to an outlet.

faq.q: Can you stop my slope from washing out?
faq.a: Usually, yes. We combine erosion control, regrading, swales or a dry creek bed, and sometimes a low retaining wall, so rain slows down and leaves the slope at a point where it will not cut a gully. Where the slope is steep, a swale or dry creek bed slows the flow.

faq.q: Do I need a French drain, or is there a simpler fix?
faq.a: Sometimes a simpler fix is enough. A downspout extension, regrading or a swale with a pop-up emitter solves many problems for far less, and small fixes like these start at $450. A French drain is the right answer when water has nowhere else to go, and we say which one yours needs. We tell you what we recommend and why in the written estimate.

fertilization.local_h: Fertilizing sand: small feedings, spread out
local: Sandy soil is the first thing to understand about a Gilmer lawn. It does not hold nutrients, so one heavy feeding mostly washes down past the roots with the next rain. Fertilizer is a waste on ground like this unless it is slow-release and spread across the season. We start with a soil sample so the plan is built from numbers, then split the feeding into several smaller rounds that the grass can pick up as it grows.

Timing matters as much as product. The first feeding goes down around April 25, once overnight lows hold above 60 degrees and the grass is fully awake. Feed in March and most of it leaves with the next rain, since Bermuda and St. Augustine are still half asleep. Round two is a summer-safe feeding in early July, and the last real nitrogen goes down in the first two weeks of September, well ahead of the first freeze.

October is a potassium month, not a nitrogen month. A winterizer with potassium helps the grass handle cold, while late nitrogen on St. Augustine feeds large patch when the nights turn damp. The big-box shelf stocks fertilizer on a northern schedule, which is wrong for East Texas. Sandy soil here also tends to run a little low on pH from years of pine needles, so we add lime only when the test calls for it.

Packed lawns get core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. That fits yards with heavy foot traffic, a truck path across the grass or a mower route that is never varied. Gilmer lawns on older lots and county acreage get the same program, and the first visit starts from about $190. Larger lawns are priced on size and number of rounds, and you see the plan in writing first. A lawn on acreage may need more rounds than a town lot.

faq.q: How often should a Gilmer lawn be fertilized?
faq.a: We run four feedings on the East Texas schedule: late April, early July, early September and a potassium winterizer in October. On sandy ground, slow-release product matters because quick-release fertilizer washes through before the grass can use it. Visits start from about $190.

faq.q: Why not just feed my lawn in March like the stores say?
faq.a: Grass is still half dormant in March and cannot take up much, so most of the fertilizer washes out in the next rain. In sandy soil it goes even faster. We wait until nights hold above 60 degrees, which is usually near the end of April.

faq.q: Do you test the soil first?
faq.a: Yes. We pull a sample, and the plan is built from the results, including whether lime is needed to correct a low pH. You get the plan and price in writing before any product goes down, so there are no surprises on the first visit.

faq.q: My lawn is packed hard. Will aeration help?
faq.a: Often it does, mostly on lawns that take heavy traffic. We core aerate between late August and mid-September and follow with a feeding so water and nutrients reach the roots. We will tell you at the walkthrough whether your lawn actually needs it, since a lawn that is not packed does not need the extra cost.

faq.q: Does the program include weed or insect treatment?
faq.a: No. We do not treat for weeds or insects. Our program covers soil testing, fertilizer, lime when needed and aeration. If weeds or insects are your main worry, that is a job for a pest control company. What we do is keep the grass itself fed and well rooted.

Before we plan the plants, we check how many hours of sun the bed gets. On older Gilmer lots, a front bed often sits under an oak or beside the porch, with only a few hours of light. Beds out on open acreage get full sun all afternoon. Shade beds can take azaleas and hydrangeas if they are sited right, while a sun bed gets lantana, salvia, plumbago and knockout roses. Native and pollinator selections are part of the mix, and we space plants so air moves through them.

Timing depends on the plant. Shrubs and perennials do best in fall, September through November, while the soil is warm and the air cools. Heat lovers like vinca wait until the soil is truly warm, usually mid-May and later. June is the clean window for hollies and boxwoods, after the spring flush, with a lighter touch-up later if the hedge needs one. Most hedges want two to three trims between spring and fall, and we can set a recurring schedule or come back when you call. We skip hard shearing in late fall, because tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap. Hollies grown for winter berries get a lighter cut, because a hard June shearing trims off berries that would color up in December.

irrigation.local_h: Designing watering for sand that dries out in days
local: Gilmer sand drains fast, which means a lawn can dry out in a few hot days. Even head-to-head coverage matters more here than almost anywhere. A gap in coverage that a clay yard would shrug off turns into a brown stripe in sand within a week. We lay out zones by sun, shade, turf and beds, so each part of the yard gets what it needs and nothing is soaked while the next section goes thirsty.

Flower beds are where most systems go wrong. Spray heads in a bed wet the leaves, the mulch and the siding and still leave the roots dry. We put drip in the beds and shrubs, so the water goes to the roots and foliage stays dry. That helps in a warm, wet spring, when fungus shows up. On rolling ground, we split zones by slope, because water runs to the low side and the high side is left short.

The controller matters as much as the pipe. Many systems are programmed once when installed and never touched again. We set the schedule for the summer, not for whenever the system went in, and show you how to change it. New automatic systems get a rain or freeze sensor, so the sprinklers do not run in a storm or a hard freeze. If you are on city water, a backflow prevention device goes in.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work, so our system work is done under a licensed irrigator who checks every zone before we call it done, and we pull the permit before we dig. We also repair what you have: broken heads and lines, leaking valves, zones that will not come on, and controllers nobody has touched since the house was built. Gilmer is an easy trip up Highway 300, and the walkthrough is free.

mulch-installation.local_h: What mulch does for sandy Gilmer soil
local: Mulch does extra work on sandy ground. Gilmer soil drains in hours and holds very little organic matter, so a bed with no cover dries out fast and bakes in the sun. A layer of hardwood slows evaporation, and as it breaks down it adds to the organic matter the soil is short on. We prep first. Edges get re-cut, weeds come out by the root, and we break up the crusted top inch of soil so rain gets down to the roots. Then the mulch goes down 1 to 1.5 inches deep, raked even and tapered off at stems and trunks. We never put fabric under it, because mulch is meant to turn into soil. Online calculators say three inches. In East Texas that sheds light rain and holds moisture against stems, and it costs you twice the mulch.

Material depends on the look and the yard. Hardwood is our usual, and cypress, cedar or dyed black or brown are options, so the color is your call. Pine straw is available on request, which suits country places with pines along the property line. On a sloping bed, heavy rain can wash loose mulch downhill, so we keep the layer even and the edges defined, and we may suggest a border to hold it, so the mulch stays on the bed.

The best window is late April through mid-May, after the spring growth flush and before the heat. The second is late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves drop and the first cold front arrives. Beds near big shade trees may need more cleanup first, since oak leaves collect in them. Where a layer of old mulch is still there, we may only top it up, which lowers the cost, and we tell you which it is when we measure.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be in Gilmer?
faq.a: About 1 to 1.5 inches of hardwood over a cleaned, edged bed. Deeper mulch sheds light rain and holds moisture against plant stems, which invites rot. In sandy soil, that thinner layer still slows evaporation and breaks down into organic matter the bed needs.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under the mulch?

faq.q: When is the best time to mulch?

sod-installation.local_h: Putting a new lawn on Gilmer sand
local: When a Gilmer lawn has been scalped, burned out or overrun with weeds, sod is the clean restart. Sand has one thing going for it: roots move through it quickly. Compost tilled into the sand also gives new roots something to hold onto. Once the sod has rooted, a Gilmer lawn on a slope is far harder for a storm to strip.

Watering makes or breaks a sod job on sand. New sod needs a deep soak every morning for the first two weeks, then a taper to deeper, less frequent watering as roots take hold. Timing is a bigger deal for oaks than for anything else here, so we plan visits by tree. East Texas has oak wilt, spread partly by beetles drawn to fresh pruning cuts in spring and early summer. We prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer. faq.q: When is the best time to prune trees and shrubs in Gilmer?
faq.a: Late winter, in February, for most trees and for crepe myrtles while they are dormant. Spring bloomers like azaleas wait until right after they flower. We avoid heavy pruning in late summer, because new growth will not harden off before the first freeze.

faq.q: Why do you prune oaks in winter?
faq.a: Oak wilt is a local problem, and beetles that spread it are drawn to fresh cuts in spring and early summer. So we prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer. If a storm breaks a limb, we cut it clean and seal the wound right away.

faq.q: My crepe myrtles were topped. Can they be fixed?
faq.a: Usually they can be improved. We thin the crowded growth, remove weak sprouts and let the main structure recover over a few seasons. If the tree is simply too big for its spot, a smaller variety is a better fix than another round of hard cuts.

faq.q: Can you remove a big tree near my house?
faq.a: No. We remove small trees and shrubs that have outgrown their spot, but not large trees close to structures. We will tell you at the walkthrough if a tree falls outside what we do, so you can call the right person for a job that size.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost?
faq.a: We quote it after a free walkthrough, usually within a day. Price follows the number and size of the plants, how much shaping or recovery pruning each needs, any small removals and how much debris we haul off. Easy access to the plants helps.
